extracted.intended_audience: architects, painters, and students of fine arts and architecture
extracted.subtask_description: Prescriptive and critical principles for architecture and the fine arts (material honesty, method, and moral character) with particular discussion of marble, imitation, and the relation of science to artistic perception. Aimed at guiding practicing artists/architects and students in making and judging work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Honesty in ornamentation / Against painted imitation
rubrics_metrics.description: Our common modes of decoration by painted imitation of various woods or marbles are culpable and base; 'there may, however, be, a kind of dishonesty even in the use of marble, if it is attempted to make the marble look like something else.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page repeatedly argues that painted imitation is morally and artistically wrong: it is dishonest, defends an untruth before the public, and should be judged on the simple test of honesty. It notes the social difficulty (many livelihoods depend on such arts) and that architects and others have defended the principle of honesty; the writer treats simplicity/ honesty of material use as a primary measure of desirableness of ornamentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate uses of marble (white for sculpture; colored for surfaces)
rubrics_metrics.description: White marble is evidently meant for sculpture, and the colored for the covering of large surfaces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ruskin likens marble to paper prepared by Nature: some is white (best adapted to sculpture), some colored (best for covering large surfaces). The colors in marble behave like a prepared palette and supply what the painter's brush would do; therefore the material's inherent character prescribes its proper use rather than arbitrary decorative mimicry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not admit imitation of natural materials (it destroys a source of knowledge)
rubrics_metrics.description: The moment we admit imitation of marble, this source of knowledge is destroyed: 'the whole field of this knowledge, which Nature intended us to possess when we were children, is hopelessly shut out from us.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because natural materials (e.g., marbles, woods) carry information—geographical, geological, botanical—widespread imitation prevents ordinary people from learning to read these 'legends' of nature. Imitation removes incentive or possibility of verification (touching, examining) and so confuses memory and local knowledge. This is presented as a cultural and educational loss as well as an aesthetic one.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imitation retards art and wastes human talent
rubrics_metrics.description: The practice of imitation retards art; 'there is not a meaner occupation for the human mind than the imitation of the stains and striae of marble and wood.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The grainer's work consumes real attention and skill in producing an effect that is essentially 'nothing' artistically; it reduces human imagination to producing knots and texture rather than color, form, or humor. The passage frames such mechanical imitation as a humiliating misuse of human faculties and a barrier to the development of true artistic powers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Artist's primary functions: to see and to feel (direct perception)
rubrics_metrics.description: The whole function of the artist in the world is to be a seeing and feeling creature; 'the work of his life is to be two-fold only: to see, to feel.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Nothing must come between Nature and the artist's sight: neither calculation nor hearsay may be allowed. The artist's witness must be eye-witness; genuineness and dominion of artistic work depend on personal perception. This is an imperative: perception and feeling (not reasoning) are the proper faculties for fine-art creation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Science and art are distinct: art deals with phenomena, science with facts
rubrics_metrics.description: Science deals exclusively with things as they are in themselves; and art exclusively with things as they affect the human senses and human soul.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Art is concerned with 'truth of aspect' (appearance and effect on humans); science with 'truth of essence' (facts and relations). While both concern truth, they operate differently and require different methods: art via perception/feeling, science via demonstration/reason. Ruskin warns against treating science as the essence of art—doing so typically leads to retrogression in artistic quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical requirements of the Renaissance central school (as prerequisites, not essence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Perspective, linear and aerial, perfect drawing and accurate light and shade in painting, and true anatomy in all representations of the human form… are the first requirements in all the work of this school.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These technical proficiencies (perspective, drawing, chiaroscuro, anatomy) are necessary competencies for certain schools (here described for the Renaissance central school). However, the text insists they should function as aids to perception and expression, not be mistaken for the essence of art—science/technique must remain subordinate to feeling and seeing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware moral corruption of style: Pride and Infidelity (Pride of Science/State/System)
rubrics_metrics.description: The moral, or immoral, elements uniting in the spirit of Central Renaissance architecture are, in the main, two—Pride and Infidelity; pride resolves itself into three main branches—Pride of Science, Pride of State, and Pride of System.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ruskin frames architectural style as morally charged: certain intellectual attitudes (vanity of science, state-glory, rigid systemizing) corrupt the spirit of architecture. This is a criterion for judging styles—their moral character—not merely formal perfection. He urges that these elements be examined and exposed when evaluating Renaissance (central) architecture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Knowledge must be subordinate and not obtrude during perception
rubrics_metrics.description: Knowledge may open the eyes, but it also seals them to thousands; if knowledge occupies the powers of contemplation when sight work is to be done, the mind retires inward and forgets the passing visible ones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ruskin cautions that learned reflection, when it becomes active during the moment of seeing, causes the artist to fix on a known fact and lose the broader succession of phenomena. Therefore an artist should keep knowledge servilely subordinate—useful, but readily 'trampled under foot' when it would entangle perception. This is both a working method and an anti-pattern warning.

rubrics_metrics.name: The artist should be educated but not learned (education vs. knowledge)
rubrics_metrics.description: An artist need not be a learned man; he ought, if possible, always to be an educated man: one who has understanding of his own uses and duties in the world and can make courteous account of his faculties and knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ruskin distinguishes education (broad, humane cultivation that enlarges the mind) from mere learning (accumulated facts that can contract and hamper perception). The ideal artist is well read in the best books and high-bred in heart and bearing, fit for the best society—but must avoid becoming the overly reflective, 'learned' man whose mind 'contracts' around facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use local/appropriate materials; scarcity and cost can be beneficial
rubrics_metrics.description: Where marble is not found, Nature has supplied other materials—clay for brick, or forest for timber—in the working of which she intends other characters of the human mind to be developed; the costliness of marble checks its common use in certain localities and is part of its interest as history.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ruskin advises using materials appropriate to their locality rather than importing or imitating foreign materials; local materials cultivate local character and advantages. Even costliness has value—scarcity contributes to the historical and cultural significance of materials. This is a practical guideline for material choice and regional integrity in building.

rubrics_metrics.name: Marble and stone carry historical and theological meaning—preserve and read it
rubrics_metrics.description: The colors of marble... record the means by which that marble has been produced, and the successive changes through which it has passed; in all their veins and zones... they narrate various legends, never untrue, of the former political state of the mountain kingdom to which they belonged.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Materials such as marble should be treated as carriers of history and sacred symbolism (theological language of stones). This is a criterion for appreciating and using stone: value its narrative and symbolic content and avoid practices (like imitation) that erase or mock that meaning.
